rules.title: AB 325 (Cartwright Act): ban on use or distribution of common pricing algorithms in restraint of trade
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade. It is also unlawful to use or distribute one while coercing another person to set or adopt a price or commercial term the algorithm recommends for the same or similar products or services in California. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including software, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. Commercial terms include level of service, availability, and output. Distribution includes selling, licensing, or providing access, including by subscription. The end consumer is not a covered person. A companion section (B&P § 16756.1) relaxes pleading: a Cartwright Act complaint only needs plausible factual allegations of a conspiracy and need not exclude the possibility of independent action. The rule applies to all products and services, including rental housing pricing.
rules.key_value: Ban on using/distributing a common pricing algorithm (uses competitor data, used by 2+ persons) as part of a conspiracy, or while coercing adoption of its recommended price/terms
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person using or distributing such an algorithm in California; not limited by building size or age.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to the end consumer of a product or service (excluded from the definition of 'person').
rules.interaction: Does not impair or limit the applicability of other antitrust laws (B&P Code § 16729(c)).
rules.citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729 (AB 325, Stats. 2025, ch. 338)
rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
rules.conflict_note: Effective date derived from the CA default rule: the bill was approved October 6, 2025 and has no urgency clause, so it takes effect January 1, 2026.
rules.penalty: Violation of the Cartwright Act, which the document describes as punishable as a crime; Cartwright Act enforcement provisions apply.

corroborating_sources.quoted_span: Businesses are expressly prohibited from using or distributing common pricing algorithms as part of an agreement to restrain trade.

plain.en: In California, since January 1, 2026, landlords and others can't use or share pricing software that uses competitor data to set rents as part of a conspiracy, or while pressuring others to adopt its prices or terms. It covers all buildings, regardless of size or age.
plain.es: En California, desde el 1 de enero de 2026, los propietarios y otras personas no pueden usar ni compartir programas de precios que usan datos de la competencia para fijar alquileres como parte de un acuerdo ilegal, ni presionando a otros para que adopten sus precios o condiciones. Aplica a todos los edificios, sin importar su tamaño o antigüedad.

rules.title: California application screening fee cap and screening-fee procedures (Civil Code 1950.6)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may charge a residential rental applicant an application screening fee of no more than the actual out-of-pocket cost of gathering information about the applicant, and in no case more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually by CPI beginning January 1, 1998). No fee may be charged when the landlord knows or should know no unit is or will soon be available. A fee may be charged only if the landlord offers either (A) a first-come process: completed applications considered in order received, written screening criteria provided with the application, the first qualifying applicant approved, and no fee charged unless the application is actually considered (fees inadvertently collected from concurrent submissions must be refunded within 7 days or, at the applicant's option, applied to another unit), or (B) a full refund to every applicant not selected, within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of submission, whichever is first. The landlord must give an itemized receipt (personally, by mail, or by agreed email), return any unused portion if no reference check or credit report is obtained, and give the applicant a copy of the credit report within 7 days of receiving it. Landlords may accept reusable screening reports under Section 1950.1. The fee is not security under Section 1950.5.
rules.key_value: Max $30 per applicant (CPI-adjusted annually since 1998), not more than actual out-of-pocket costs; refund to non-selected applicants within 7 days of selection/30 days of submission unless first-come screening offered; itemized receipt; credit report copy within 7 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to applicants (including guarantors/cosigners) for any residential rental property in California.
rules.exemptions: Section does not preempt provisions or regulations governing collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs. No refund required for an applicant denied after consideration for failing the landlord's established screening criteria (first-come option).
rules.interaction: Operates notwithstanding Civil Code 1950.5; screening fee is not 'security' under 1950.5 nor an 'advance fee' under Bus. & Prof. Code 10026. Landlord may accept a reusable screening report under Civil Code 1950.1.

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act – just cause for termination of tenancy
rules.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the unit for 12 months (or, if adult tenants were added before 24 months, all tenants for 12 months or one tenant for 24 months), the owner may not terminate the tenancy without an at-fault or no-fault just cause, which must be stated in the written termination notice. Curable lease violations require a notice and opportunity to cure first. For no-fault terminations (owner/relative move-in, withdrawal from rental market, government order, demolition or substantial remodel), the owner must either pay relocation assistance equal to one month's rent within 15 calendar days of service of the notice or waive the final month's rent, and must tell the tenant of this right in the notice. Owner move-in requires that the intended occupant move in within 90 days and live there 12 months, or the unit must be re-offered at the same rent with reimbursement of moving expenses. Substantial remodel notices must include specified statements, a description of the work and permits. Owners must give tenants a specified notice of these protections in at least 12-point type. Waivers are void.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 12 months of occupancy; no-fault terminations require relocation assistance or rent waiver equal to one month's rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property where the tenant has occupied 12+ months; excludes housing with a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years and property covered by a local just cause ordinance (pre-9/1/2019, or later and more protective).
rules.exemptions: Transient/tourist hotels; nonprofit hospitals, religious, extended care, licensed elder/adult residential facilities; school/university dormitories; units where tenant shares bath or kitchen with resident owner; single-family owner-occupied residences renting no more than two units or bedrooms (including ADU/JADU) and mobilehomes; owner-occupied duplex (owner occupied one unit at start of tenancy and continues); housing with certificate of occupancy within previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome); separately alienable units (e.g., single-family homes, condos) not owned by a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, if tenants received the statutory exemption notice; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; homeowners of mobilehomes; property subject to a qualifying local just cause ordinance.
rules.interaction: Does not apply where a local just cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019 applies, or where a later-adopted or amended local ordinance is more protective (with a binding local finding), in which case the local ordinance applies. A property cannot be subject to both. Local ordinances adopted after September 1, 2019 that are less protective may not be enforced unless this section is repealed. Relocation assistance under this section is credited against relocation required by other law. Yields where a covering local rule of the same category applies: r-0014, r-0015, r-0020, r-0021, r-0022, r-0023, r-0024, r-0028, r-0030, r-0031, r-0032, r-0037, r-0038.
rules.quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
rules.conflict_note: The document states this version of the section became operative April 1, 2024, and was most recently amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 203 (AB 1529), effective January 1, 2026. The core 12-month just cause requirement dates from the original Tenant Protection Act (2020), but the document does not state that date. The section sunsets and is repealed as of January 1, 2030. Subdivision (i)(3) bars enforcement of local just cause ordinances adopted after September 1, 2019 that are less protective than this section. That is a partial preemption of weaker local rules, which a reviewer should verify against each city ordinance.
rules.penalty: Termination notice void for noncompliance (and for failure to strictly comply with relocation rules); owner who attempts to recover possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, discretionary attorney's fees and costs, up to treble damages for willful/oppressive/fraudulent/malicious conduct, and punitive damages; Attorney General, city attorney or county counsel may seek injunctive relief.

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act statewide rent cap
rules.requirement: An owner may not raise the gross rent more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living (regional CPI-U), or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period. The cap is measured from the lowest gross rent charged in the prior 12 months, excluding discounts and concessions. No more than two increases are allowed in 12 months for the same tenant. Vacancy decontrol applies: the owner may set the initial rent for a new tenancy. Rent increase notice must be given under Section 827. Waivers are void. The section sunsets January 1, 2030.
rules.key_value: 5% + CPI, max 10% per 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property except housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (mobilehomes excepted from that exemption), units under stricter local rent control, and other listed exemptions.
rules.exemptions: The cap does not apply to: (1) deed- or regulatory-restricted affordable housing, or housing under an affordable-housing subsidy agreement; (2) school or university dormitories; (3) housing under local rent control that restricts annual increases below the state cap; (4) housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless a mobilehome; (5) separately alienable units (e.g., single-family homes and condos) not owned by a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member, if the required exemption notice was given; (6) an owner-occupied two-unit property where neither unit is an ADU or JADU; (7) homeowners of mobilehomes.
rules.interaction: Does not apply to housing under valid local rent control (consistent with Costa-Hawkins, Civ. Code 1954.50 et seq.) that restricts annual increases below the state cap. rules.title: FEHA screening limits: source of income (incl. Section 8) and criminal history
rules.requirement: Housing providers, including tenant screening companies, may not refuse to rent or set different terms based on source of income. This covers Housing Choice (Section 8) vouchers and other rental assistance, and includes refusing to complete program paperwork or advertising 'No Section 8.' Providers may check criminal history but may not consider arrests that did not lead to a conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile records. Blanket bans on applicants with any criminal history are prohibited. A denial based on a conviction must rest on a conviction directly related to tenancy, considering the nature and severity of the offense and the time elapsed.
rules.key_value: No source-of-income (incl. Section 8) discrimination; no blanket criminal-history bans; no use of non-conviction arrests, sealed/expunged or juvenile records
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most housing accommodations and housing providers in California, including landlords and tenant screening companies.
rules.exemptions: An owner occupying a home and renting to one additional person may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics, but may not publish discriminatory statements or ads. Shared living areas in a single dwelling may be limited to one sex. Qualifying senior housing may be limited by age.
rules.interaction: Local ordinances may impose stricter criminal-history or source-of-income screening limits.
rules.citation: Cal. Gov. Code § 12900 et seq. (Fair Employment and Housing Act)
rules.quoted_span: California law protects tenants from discrimination based on how a tenant will be paying rent (“source of income”). This includes the State of California’s COVID-19 Rent Relief Program, Housing Choice (Section 8) vouchers
rules.penalty: Remedies include out-of-pocket losses, injunction, access to the denied housing, emotional distress damages, civil penalties or punitive damages, and attorney's fees. Complaint to CRD within one year, or court action within two years.

plain.en: In California, landlords and screening companies cannot turn you down or treat you differently because you use Section 8 or other rental help. They cannot ban everyone with a record or use arrests without convictions, sealed records, or juvenile records. Some owner-occupied homes are exempt.
plain.es: En California, los propietarios y las empresas de evaluación no pueden rechazarle ni darle otras condiciones por usar la Sección 8 u otra ayuda para el alquiler. Tampoco pueden rechazar a toda persona con antecedentes ni usar arrestos sin condena, registros sellados o de menores. Algunas viviendas donde vive el dueño están exentas.

rules.title: California FEHA housing discrimination: source-of-income protection and credit-history alternatives for subsidized applicants
rules.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against applicants or tenants based on source of income. Source of income means lawful, verifiable income, including public assistance and housing subsidies such as Section 8 vouchers and HUD-VASH vouchers. Owners may not publish ads stating a source-of-income preference or limitation. Income standards must count the combined income of people who will live together, on the same basis as married couples. Where there is a government rent subsidy, owners must apply income standards only to the tenant's share of the rent. They also may not use credit history unless they offer the applicant the option of providing alternative evidence of ability to pay that share, such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements. They must give reasonable time to provide that evidence and must reasonably consider it in place of credit history. Owners may still ask about the level or source of income, verify employment, request landlord references, and verify identity.
rules.key_value: Source-of-income discrimination (including Section 8/HUD-VASH vouchers) prohibited; for subsidized applicants, income tests apply only to the tenant's rent portion and alternative evidence must be accepted in lieu of credit history
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to owners of housing accommodations in California. The subsidy-specific provisions apply where the applicant has a government rent subsidy.
rules.exemptions: An inquiry about the level or source of income is not source-of-income discrimination. Owners may still verify employment, request landlord references, and verify identity. A landlord is not considered a tenant's representative unless the income is a HUD-VASH voucher.

rules.title: California security deposit limits and return rules (Civil Code 1950.5)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security, however labeled, of more than one month's rent on top of first month's rent. A small landlord may charge up to two months' rent if it is a natural person, or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, and owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than 4 units in total. That exception does not apply to service member tenants. An advance payment of at least six months' rent is allowed on leases of six months or longer. Since April 1, 2025, a higher deposit charged to a service member must be explained in writing and returned after 6 months without rent arrears. Deductions are limited to unpaid rent, tenant-caused damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning to move-in condition, and restoring personal property. The tenant may request an initial pre-move-out inspection and must receive an itemized statement of proposed deductions. Landlords must photograph the unit at move-in (tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025), after move-out, and after repairs. Within 21 calendar days after move-out, the landlord must give an itemized statement with receipts and invoices and return the balance, electronically if the deposit or rent was paid electronically. On sale or transfer, the deposit must be transferred to the successor or returned. Deposits may not be called nonrefundable.
rules.key_value: Max deposit = 1 month's rent (2 months for qualifying small natural-person landlords); return within 21 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to security for any residential rental used as the tenant's dwelling. The 2-month cap applies only if the landlord is a natural person or an all-natural-person LLC owning no more than two rental properties with no more than 4 units in total, and never to service member tenants.
rules.exemptions: The cap does not apply to security collected or demanded before July 1, 2024. Advance payment of at least 6 months' rent is permitted for leases of 6+ months. Fees for tenant-requested alterations are permitted. Application screening fees fall under Section 1950.6. Inspection requirements do not apply to terminations under CCP 1161(2)-(4). Documentation requirements do not apply if deductions are $125 or less or the tenant validly waived them.

rules.penalty: Bad faith retention or claim may result in statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security plus actual damages. A landlord who in bad faith fails to comply with the itemization and return rules forfeits any claim to the security.

rules.title: Prohibition on the Sale or Use of Coordinated Pricing Algorithms to Set Rents or Manage Occupancy Levels (Ord. 7,992-N.S.)
rules.requirement: Landlords may not use a coordinated pricing algorithm when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential units in Berkeley. No one may sell, license or otherwise provide such an algorithm to Berkeley landlords. A coordinated pricing algorithm is any process that uses nonpublic Competitor Data (data less than 90 days old about properties the landlord does not own or manage) to calculate and recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms in coordination among competing landlords, including through a third-party vendor. Each month and each unit is a separate violation. The chapter does not regulate the amount of rent.
rules.key_value: Ban on landlord use and on sale/licensing of coordinated pricing algorithms using nonpublic competitor data (<90 days old); up to $1,000 civil penalty per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: All residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley; applies to landlords and to vendors that provide algorithms to Berkeley landlords.
rules.exemptions: Excluded from the definition: aggregated, anonymous rental data reports that do not recommend rents or terms; products used to set rent or income limits under government affordable housing guidelines; market research for project financing, appraisals, and research, testing or training for software development (if competitor data is not an input when a recommendation is calculated). Software using public data is not restricted.

rules.requirement: Landlords may not ask about or use criminal history or criminal background checks in rental advertising, applications, tenant selection or decision-making. Any adverse action based on criminal history requires written notice and an opportunity to respond. rules.title: Los Angeles Just Cause Ordinance (JCO)
rules.requirement: Landlords may terminate tenancies only for listed just causes. At-fault causes include nonpayment, failure to cure a lease violation, nuisance or damage, illegal use, refusal to renew a similar agreement, denial of reasonable access, and an unapproved subtenant at lease end. No-fault causes include owner or family move-in, a required resident manager, demolition, removal from the rental market or conversion to non-residential use, a government order to vacate, a HUD sale, residential hotel conversion or demolition, and conversion to affordable housing. Landlords must pay relocation assistance for no-fault evictions. Applies to tenancies once the tenant has lived in the unit 6 months or the original lease has expired, whichever comes first.

rules.title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protections Ordinance (just cause and relocation assistance)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a tenancy without just cause. At-fault causes include nonpayment, material lease breach after a written cure notice, nuisance, waste, refusal to renew on similar terms, criminal activity or threats, unauthorized sublet, refusal of lawful entry, unlawful use, an employee failing to vacate, and failure to deliver possession after the tenant's own notice. No-fault causes include owner or family move-in (allowed for leases from 6/24/2023 only if the lease permits it or the tenant agrees in writing; the occupant must move in within 90 days and stay 12 months), withdrawal from the rental market, a government order to vacate for 30+ days, and demolition or substantial remodel (permits must be obtained first and the notice certified under penalty of perjury). For no-fault terminations the landlord must give 30/60-day written notice under Civ. Code 1946.1 stating the basis, and must provide relocation assistance regardless of tenant income or tenancy length. Assistance is 2 months' actual rent (3 months if the tenant is a senior or disabled), paid within 15 days of notice or given as a rent waiver. Displaced tenants have a 5-year right of first refusal if the unit is re-rented after an owner move-in, government order or remodel/demolition termination. The landlord must notify the Housing Commission within 3 business days of at-fault and no-fault terminations once its portal exists. Buyout agreements must exceed the relocation amount and meet disclosure rules, or they are void. Noncompliance voids the termination notice.
rules.key_value: Just cause required for all terminations; no-fault relocation assistance of 2 months' rent (3 months for seniors/disabled)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property in San Diego, except buildings issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (mobilehomes excepted) and other listed exemptions.
rules.exemptions: Transient/tourist hotel occupancy; short-term residential occupancy; deed- or agreement-restricted affordable housing and subsidized affordable housing (Section 8 not exempt); mobilehomes under the Mobilehome Residency Law; nonprofit hospital, religious, care facilities and nonprofit transitional housing; school/college dormitories; units where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with a resident landlord; owner-occupied single-family residence (including renting up to two bedrooms/ADUs/JADUs); owner-occupied duplex; housing with a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable units (e.g., single-family homes/condos) whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, with the required written exemption notice (in the lease for tenancies from 1/1/2024). Tenancies of 30 days or less and fixed-term leases of 3 months or less are not tenancies.
rules.interaction: Local ordinance adopted consistent with Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2; rights are in addition to state and federal law. Relocation assistance is credited against relocation assistance required by other federal, state or local law.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause eviction requirement
rules.requirement: To evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have one of 17 listed just cause reasons, and it must be the dominant motive for the eviction. The listed causes include nonpayment or habitual late payment, an uncured substantial breach, nuisance, illegal use, refusal to renew on like terms, refusal of access, an unapproved subtenant, owner or family move-in, condo conversion sale, demolition or permanent removal, temporary capital improvements, substantial rehabilitation, Ellis Act withdrawal, lead remediation, a development agreement, an expired Good Samaritan tenancy, and a Planning Code Sec. 317 development project. Expiration of the lease or a change in ownership is not just cause. A just cause reason is also needed to remove housing services such as parking, storage or laundry, except temporary removal for mandatory soft-story seismic retrofit under Sec. 37.2(r). Eviction protections cover units built after June 13, 1979 that are exempt from the rent increase limits, Costa-Hawkins-exempt tenancies, and some government-regulated tenancies.

rules.coverage_conditions: Rental units covered by the SF Rent Ordinance, including units exempt from rent increase limits (post-June 13, 1979 certificate of occupancy, Costa-Hawkins units).
rules.exemptions: Units not covered by the Rent Ordinance (exemption categories are not detailed in this document).
rules.interaction: Applies to units exempt from the city's rent increase limits under Costa-Hawkins and to new construction.

rules.penalty: Landlord who evicts or tries to evict unlawfully may be subject to substantial civil and/or criminal liability.

rules.title: Statewide prohibition on local rent control (G.L. c.40P § 4)
rules.requirement: No Massachusetts city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind. The only exception is for a municipality that accepts chapter 40P. It also may not apply to units of owners with fewer than ten rental units or to units with fair market rent over $400. Third, the municipality must pay owners, from general funds, the difference between fair market rent and the controlled rent.

rules.title: Massachusetts security deposit law
rules.requirement: A security deposit may not exceed one month's rent. It must be held in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, beyond the reach of the lessor's creditors. The lessor must give: a receipt for the deposit; a statement of condition within 10 days of tenancy start; and a bank receipt within 30 days. Tenants earn 5% interest per year (or the lesser rate the bank pays), paid annually; the same interest rule applies to last month's rent paid in advance. The lessor must keep deposit records for 2 years. The deposit must be returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Allowed deductions are limited to unpaid rent or water charges, tax-escalation amounts, and reasonable repair of tenant-caused damage (excluding reasonable wear and tear), backed by a sworn itemized list. The deposit must be transferred to a buyer or other successor owner. Lease waivers of these rules are void. EOHLC may adopt regulations allowing an optional fee in lieu of a deposit, capped at 1 month's rent in total.

Failure to pay interest within 30 days of termination brings treble interest damages plus costs and fees. Failure to give the bank receipt, or to make records available, entitles the tenant to immediate return of the deposit.

rules.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (criminal history and credit screening limits for DND-funded / IDP income-restricted housing)

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: Makes it unlawful under the New Jersey Antitrust Act for a rental property owner (or its agent) to pay for or use the services of a coordinator. A coordinator is an operator of algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that performs a coordinating function: using two or more owners' nonpublic competitively sensitive information to set or recommend rents, lease terms or occupancy, or setting or recommending rents for multiple owners through the same algorithm. Coordinators may not facilitate anticompetitive agreements, and no person may engage in parallel pricing coordination or perform a coordinating function. Exclusions cover research, free public rent estimates, equal-access brokerage listing databases that do not set or recommend prices, and government affordability controls. The Attorney General must set up a complaint portal and may adopt rules.

rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about an applicant's criminal record, orally, in writing or on an application, until after a conditional offer. Exceptions: lifetime sex-offender registration and methamphetamine production on federally assisted housing premises. Providers may never consider arrests or charges without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. After a conditional offer, they may consider only: listed serious convictions (murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, etc.) or lifetime sex-offender registration; first-degree offenses within 6 years; second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years; and fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. A conditional offer may be withdrawn only if, after an individualized assessment of listed factors, withdrawal is necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest (preponderance of the evidence). Withdrawal requires a written notice stating the reasons and giving an opportunity to appeal. On request within 30 days, the provider must give the applicant a free copy of the information it relied on within 10 days. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is considered and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracy or rehabilitation. Ads stating that people with arrests or convictions will not be considered are prohibited. Requiring drug or alcohol tests, or consent to obtain drug-treatment records, is prohibited.

rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental dwelling units other than units in owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.
rules.exemptions: Dwelling units in owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units. Inquiry is allowed on lifetime sex-offender registration and on methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted housing premises.
rules.interaction: Enforced only through complaints to the NJ Division on Civil Rights; no private court action. Rights under the NJ Law Against Discrimination (C.10:5-1 et seq.) are preserved.

rules.title: Security Deposit Law – cap, interest, notices and 30-day return
rules.requirement: The security deposit may not exceed 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid or last month's rent and any pet deposit count toward the cap, so no more than 2.5 months' rent may be collected at lease inception, including first month's rent. Deposits must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account at a New Jersey institution, with interest belonging to the tenant and paid annually or credited to rent. The landlord must give written notice of the bank, amount, account type and interest rate within 30 days of receipt and annually. If notice or interest is not provided, the tenant may apply the deposit plus 7% interest to rent. The deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions, must be returned within 30 days after termination by personal delivery, registered or certified mail. It must be returned within 5 business days if the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation. A new owner is responsible for the deposit.
rules.key_value: Max 1.5x monthly rent; return within 30 days with interest and itemized deductions
rules.coverage_conditions: Most residential rental properties, including mobile homes. Excludes owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings unless the tenant opts in.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, unless the tenant makes the law applicable by written request (effective 30 days later). Seasonal rentals of 125 days or less are exempt from the investment and interest provisions.
rules.quoted_span: one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ). It can be less.
rules.penalty: Double the amount wrongfully withheld plus court costs and reasonable attorney fees (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1). Civil penalty of $500-$2,000 per offense for willfully withholding deposits of assisted tenants (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.5). Disorderly persons offense for unlawful use of deposit monies: fine of at least $200 and/or up to 30 days imprisonment (N.J.S.A. 46:8-25).

No aplica a viviendas de dos o tres unidades donde vive el dueño.
